output:
Here's the draft. I've written it as a proper document with headings, kept the jokes coming from your own stories, and put the calling instructions and fridge checklist in as you asked. There are a few blanks in square brackets for you to fill in before it goes in the folder.

---

# Helping Your Midwife Find You

**Riverside Community Midwives — Home Birth Welcome Pack**

## First, a quick word about who we are

There's a saying in the Philippines that a midwife is like family. We borrowed it, because it's true and it's the best thing anyone has ever said about us.

When we come to your house for your baby's birth, we are not visitors. We are the people you've been talking to for months, the people who have heard you say "I'm scared" and "I don't think I can do this" and "what if I change my mind?" We come in as friends, and we stay until you're both okay.

So this page is not a list of instructions to be obeyed. It's a list of the things that help us get to you quickly when it's dark and it's raining and you're in labour and everything feels too big. Read it once now, when you're calm. Stick the checklist on the fridge. Then forget about it until you need us.

## The one date that matters: 37 weeks

**Home birth cover starts at 37 weeks.**

Before 37 weeks, if baby decides to come, you go to the hospital — not your house. We say this at booking, and then everybody forgets it, because 37 weeks feels like ages away right up until the week it isn't. Write it on the fridge. Circle it. Put it in your phone.

Once you reach 37 weeks, home birth is on, unless your midwife talks to you and says otherwise.

## When labour starts: phone the birth line

**As soon as you think labour has started, ring the Riverside birth line:**

### 📞 **[BIRTH LINE NUMBER]**

That's also on the front of your welcome pack, and on the back of the checklist on your fridge.

A few important things about that call:

- **Please use the birth line, not my personal mobile.** I know I've been Liberal with my number. It's for forms, questions, the birth pool, and the odd "sorry, is Thursday right?" — but it's not the number for labour. The birth line goes to whoever is on call that night, and that is exactly the person who will come to you. It's also how we get the second midwife moving.
- **Don't wait for a routine check-in.** If you think it's happening, ring. You can ring at 2am with a question and we will be completely normal about it.
- **If you're not sure it's real labour, ring anyway.** Nobody minds. A phone call in the small hours is a very small thing compared with what we might be doing in your house an hour later.
- **If you can't get through and you think you need us urgently, call 999** and ask for the midwife on call. For non-emergency advice, NHS 111.

Sometimes the safest place for you and baby to be is the birth centre. If we ever say "come in", that is not a failure and nothing to feel bad about. It's us doing the job properly.

## What we bring, and why we need a bit of room

We bring a lot. Gas and air cylinders. The big bag. Pool equipment if you're planning a birth pool. Newborn and resuscitation kit. We carry it in, and sometimes up, and our arms get very tired indeed.

So, two small favours:

**One — please leave us two parking spaces if you can.** Two midwives usually come for a birth, and we usually come in separate cars. If there's only one space, don't rearrange your life — tell us and we'll manage. But two spaces means two midwives who aren't walking round the block carrying a cylinder each.

**Two — if you have a driveway, an alley, a side gate, or a way to get close to the door, please tell us.** Some of our favourite births have happened in houses with no driveway at all.

If you're having a pool birth, mention it at booking so we bring the right kit. It needs more space and more set-up time than people expect.

## Parking and permit zones

Some streets around **Anfield** and **Kensington** are in parking permit zones. If yours is one of them, you've got two options:

- **Apply for a council visitor permit**, or
- **Leave our vehicle details on the dashboard** so we can display them — our registration(s) are **[REG]** and **[REG]**.

If you'd rather apply for a permit for one of our cars, ring the team and we'll tell you which car is coming and what the registration is. Do that before 37 weeks, not on the night.

We have got parking tickets before, and we paid them, but it was our money and we'd rather spend it on gas and air.

## Helping us find your actual front door

This is the bit that saves us twenty minutes. Twenty minutes matters when you're in labour.

**House numbers.** Put your number somewhere visible from the road — on the gate, on the wall, on the door, high up if you can. If your house has a name and no number (*Rosemary Cottage* in a street of terraces, we know the one), we love a name, but please also give us a number or the nearest numbered house and which side of the street it's on, plus one landmark. Last time we confidently parked outside a chippy and were sent to the wrong cottage entirely.

**Blocks of flats.** Which block, which floor, which entrance, and does the lift work at 3am? Yes, the lift is sometimes the problem and not the door. I once spent twenty minutes going round a block in Everton hunting for flat 14, and flat 14 was not near flat 13 — it was in a different building, different entrance. In the end the dad was waving a tea towel out of the window. **Wave the tea towel.** It works, and it's lovely.

**Terraces.** They all look the same. Tell us which side the front is on. Red door? Blue gate? Wheelie bin? Postbox? The postbox, honestly, is usually the most reliable thing in England.

**Villages and quiet streets.** Give us one landmark — the pub with the red sign, the church, the petrol station, the football pitch.

**Two front doors?** Say which one is yours and we'll split up.

## Send us a pin

If you can, **send a pin drop on WhatsApp to the birth line number** once you've got the place in view. It's the fastest way to get us to the right door.

**what3words** works beautifully too, if you're used to it — three words that pin your front door to a spot on the map, which is far more reliable than a postcode for the last fifty yards. Send it to the birth line, so whoever is on call has it in front of them.

## Lights, gates and other excellent ideas

- **Put your porch light on.** Please. Dark streets in winter all look the same, and a lit porch says *this is the one*.
- **Balloons on the gate.** One family did this and we found them first time, no faffing, no circling the block. We still talk about it. We call it the best idea we've ever had, and we would like every family to know it's available to them. If you want to be the family in the next version of this story, that is the way.
- **Leave the outside light and the hall light on** until we're in.
- **Gate codes, door codes, alarms.** Tell us the code, or how to switch it off, so we can get in without you having to get out of bed. Whatever you tell us stays with us.
- **Charged phone, on loud.** Not just for us. For you, to call us, and for taking the photo of the first hour.

## Getting through the door

Please clear a route from the front door to the room you want to birth in — **hallway, stairs, landing, door.** Shoes off the stairs. Washing basket off the landing. Lego off the stairs. All of it, every time, and I am sorry if your house is a Lego house, mine was too.

This isn't about being fussy. It's so we can get to you quickly, keep the floor clean, and get our hands washed properly before we touch you and your baby.

## Dogs, cats and other housemates

We love dogs. Genuinely, we do.

**But please put them in another room with a door on before we arrive.** Not because we don't want to meet them — because a friendly dog having a wonderful time in the middle of a birth is a distraction for everybody, and nobody needs a dog in the room mid-contraction. Put water down, and we'll say hello properly afterwards.

(Our own staffie, Pippin, loves me rather too much. She jumped up on me at a visit once and I nearly dropped the Entonox cylinder. Pippin has been formally spoken to.)

## If we still get it wrong

Doors get opened. Once I knocked on the wrong house, the door was open, and a lovely old man handed me a Jammie Dodger and wished me luck. So: if we turn up in the wrong place, we're sorry and we'll move on quickly.

But for your protection, please **don't open your door to every knock** if you're expecting us. Put your name and postcode on a card in the window, or a note on the door: *"Flat 3 — midwife expected."* And if you can, leave a key with a neighbour or in a key safe so we can get in if you're in the bathroom when we arrive.

## Things that are lovely to have ready

Not required, and don't go shopping. But if they're already in the house, we will be glad of:

- Clean towels, a couple of spare sheets
- A big bin bag or two, and a bucket
- A torch — a head torch or your phone
- Snacks and a flask for us. We're usually there a while and we don't get to nip out. Sandwiches are, frankly, the highlight of our shift.
- Your birth notes, birth plan, and a pen
- A chair for me, and a table within reach of the birth pool if you're using one

---

# 📋 Fridge checklist

**Print this, stick it on the fridge, and tick it as you go.**

**Before 37 weeks**
- ☐ Date 37 weeks is written on the calendar: **____/____/____**
- ☐ Birth line number written down: **[BIRTH LINE NUMBER]**
- ☐ Parking: two spaces kept clear; permit applied for or details on dashboard
- ☐ Driveway / alley / side entrance? We'll be told
- ☐ House number visible from the road
- ☐ Flat? Block, floor, entrance, and does the lift work at night
- ☐ Gate code / alarm code written on the card below
- ☐ what3words code or a pin ready to send
- ☐ Porch light working — and a spare bulb
- ☐ Hallway and stairs clear: no shoes, no washing basket, no Lego
- ☐ Towels, bucket, bin bags, torch, snacks for the midwives
- ☐ Phone charged and set to ring loudly
- ☐ Dog's room sorted, water down
- ☐ Name and postcode card in the window

**When labour starts**
- ☐ Phone the **Riverside birth line** on **[BIRTH LINE NUMBER]**
- ☐ Not a personal mobile — the birth line, so the on-call midwife gets it
- ☐ Send a pin or what3words to the birth line
- ☐ Porch light on, gate code ready
- ☐ Midwives have room to park and a clear path in
- ☐ Phone on loud, keys to hand

---

**Useful numbers**

| Who | Number |
|---|---|
| Riverside birth line (labour, 24 hours) | **[BIRTH LINE NUMBER]** |
| Riverside team office (admin, forms, booking) | **[OFFICE NUMBER]** |
| Urgent / emergency | **999** |
| NHS advice line | **111** |

*Your midwife's name is **[NAME]**. Her mobile is for practical questions only — for labour, please use the birth line.*

---

## A couple of notes before you print it

**Things I've left blank for you to fill in:** the birth line number, office number, your name, the two vehicle registrations, and the 37-week date (which each family will write in themselves).

**Two things worth checking with Deb or the clinical lead before it goes out:** the exact visitor permit wording for Liverpool City Council — I've kept it deliberately loose ("apply for a visitor permit, or leave our vehicle details on the dashboard") because council schemes change, and it's easier to lock that down yourself. And the line about the birth centre being the safest place sometimes, which is standard and reassuring but isn't from your notes — delete it if you'd rather keep that in a different part of the pack.

**For Facebook:** rather than posting the whole thing as a wall of text, post the fridge checklist on its own as a picture, with a line like *"New to Riverside home birth? This is everything we need to find you in a hurry — photo and stick it on your fridge. Full version's in the welcome pack."* The Everton flat and the chippy stories tend to do better on there than the parking permit bit, so maybe lead with the funny half and point people to the pack for the rest.
